Incorrect RFC 3986 URI serialization for oversized input.

The Uri\Rfc3986\Uri class does not correctly handle the output-size limit and errors of the uriparser library when converting a URI back to a string. For a URI whose string representation reaches approximately 2 GiB, toString(), toRawString() and other serializing operations can return a truncated or invalid string instead of an error. An application that accepts attacker-controlled URI data of that size, has enough memory to process it and trusts the result may make incorrect validation or routing decisions, and the large allocations can exhaust memory. parse_url() and Uri\WhatWg\Url are not affected.

This issue affects PHP versions 8.5.* before 8.5.13.

Use-after-free in magic method backtraces can lead to remote code execution.

When collecting the arguments of a method call handled by __call() or __callStatic() for a backtrace, PHP can read stale values that may refer to freed memory. If a fatal error such as exceeding memory_limit occurs while an application enters such a call, with fatal_error_backtraces enabled (the default) and zend.exception_ignore_args disabled, a remote attacker who controls enough request data to influence memory allocation may cause memory corruption, crash the PHP worker or, with knowledge of memory addresses, execute arbitrary code. php.ini-production enables zend.exception_ignore_args, which prevents this.

This issue affects PHP versions 8.5.* before 8.5.13.

Use-after-free after interrupted session shutdown.

The session extension records the filename of the executing script when a session starts. If a fatal error occurs in an application callback while the session variables are destroyed at shutdown, such as stream_close() of a user-defined stream wrapper, the pointer is retained after the request memory is freed, and a later request handled by the same worker can free the stale string. An attacker who can trigger such a failing cleanup may crash the worker or corrupt memory; code execution has not been demonstrated. This requires the filename to be allocated in request memory, for example when the script is not cached by OPcache.

This issue affects PHP versions 8.3.* before 8.3.37, 8.4.* before 8.4.28 and 8.5.* before 8.5.13.

Timezone cache use-after-free can lead to remote code execution.

In non-thread-safe builds, a diagnostic written to a file-based error_log during module startup, for example for an invalid date.timezone value or a session configuration warning, causes the timezone cache to be allocated in startup memory that is freed while a reference to it is kept. A diagnostic raised early in the first request of a worker, such as the max_input_vars warning, then accesses the freed cache. On such a deployment an unauthenticated remote attacker can crash PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php or CGI workers with a crafted request. Arbitrary code execution may be possible and has been demonstrated with known memory addresses.

This issue affects PHP versions before 8.2.36, 8.3.* before 8.3.37, 8.4.* before 8.4.28 and 8.5.* before 8.5.13.

@fastify/http-proxy is a Fastify plugin that proxies HTTP and WebSocket traffic to an upstream server. In versions from 9.0.0 up to but not including 11.6.10, when the plugin is registered with websocket support enabled, it takes every upgraded socket and dispatches the request through the Fastify router before the WebSocket library takes ownership of the socket. Node.js removes its own error listener from the socket before emitting the upgrade event, and the plugin does not attach one of its own during routing, so a socket error such as a client connection reset that arrives before the WebSocket library takes over is unhandled and terminates the Node.js process. The error window is open whenever anything asynchronous runs between dispatch and the route handler, such as an async hook on the proxied route or any unrelated async route in the application. A single unauthenticated upgrade request followed by a connection reset is enough to crash the server, and it can be repeated to keep the process down. The issue is fixed in @fastify/http-proxy 11.6.10, and users should upgrade to 11.6.10 or later.

Double free during DOM XML serialization.

The XML serializer of Dom\XMLDocument and Dom\HTMLDocument can share ownership of a generated namespace prefix between the namespace-prefix maps of an element and a descendant, so the prefix is used after being freed and then freed a second time. The document does not need to be malformed. An application that parses attacker-controlled XML or HTML with these classes and serializes it with saveXml() can be crashed, and repeated requests can cause denial of service. Code execution has not been demonstrated.

This issue affects PHP versions 8.4.* before 8.4.28 and 8.5.* before 8.5.13.

@fastify/http-proxy is a Fastify plugin that proxies HTTP and WebSocket traffic to an upstream server. In versions from 9.4.0 up to but not including 11.6.10, when the plugin is registered with websocket support enabled, a WebSocket upgrade request whose path carries a URL fragment is matched by the router and answered with a successful upgrade before the upstream link is created. Building the upstream target then throws, the error is only logged, and the accepted client socket is left open with no error listener, so the next frame the client sends becomes an unhandled error and terminates the Node.js process. A request target that is not a valid URL reference reaching a parameterized prefix triggers the same path. A single unauthenticated upgrade request followed by one frame is enough to crash the server, and it can be repeated to keep the process down. The issue is fixed in @fastify/http-proxy 11.6.10, and users should upgrade to 11.6.10 or later.

SOAP use-after-free when processing DTD entity references.

The SOAP extension frees the document type definition (DTD) of a parsed XML document while attribute values can still refer to entities it owns, and can then read freed memory. Removing the DTD also bypasses the SOAP server's rejection of documents that contain one. An unauthenticated remote attacker who can send a crafted request to a SOAP endpoint, or who controls a WSDL or schema document loaded by the application, can crash the PHP process and cause denial of service. Memory disclosure and code execution have not been confirmed.

This issue affects PHP versions before 8.2.36, 8.3.* before 8.3.37, 8.4.* before 8.4.28 and 8.5.* before 8.5.13.

In the Apache Airflow Microsoft Azure provider 10.2.0 through 15.3.0, `S3ToAzureBlobStorageOperator` turned off TLS certificate verification for its connection to Amazon S3 by default (`s3_verify=False`), whatever the AWS connection's own verification settings were. An attacker positioned on the network between an Airflow worker and S3 could intercept that traffic, read the signed requests and alter the listed object keys and the copied file contents. Deployments are affected when a Dag uses `S3ToAzureBlobStorageOperator` without setting `s3_verify`. Users are advised to upgrade to apache-airflow-providers-microsoft-azure 15.3.1 or later, which uses the AWS connection's verification settings by default.

Improper Output Neutralization for Logs vulnerability in the XmlLayout and XmlLayoutSchemaLog4J of Apache log4net.

Both layouts split a message holding the CDATA end marker into several CDATA sections, but searched for the marker with a culture-sensitive comparison. Ignorable characters or a combining mark around the marker made the search miss it, so the CDATA section stayed open. From 3.3.1 on, an XML parser then reads the following log events as part of that message; earlier versions leave the log file not well-formed. A party whose data reaches a log message could hide later log events from a consumer that parses the XML log.

This issue affects Apache log4net: from 1.2.9 before 3.6.0.

Users are recommended to upgrade to version 3.6.0, which fixes the issue.

Improper Output Neutralization for Logs vulnerability in the FileAppender, RollingFileAppender, UdpAppender and SmtpAppender of Apache log4net.

Characters the configured encoding could not represent were converted by that encoding's best-fit fallback, which turns fullwidth characters such as U+FF1C, U+FF1E and U+FF02 into <, > and ". The conversion happened after XmlLayout or XmlLayoutSchemaLog4J had escaped the text, so a party whose data reaches a log message could forge complete log events in an XML log, for example a fake audit entry. On .NET Framework this needs no configuration where the ANSI code page is single-byte, since that is the default encoding; on .NET it needs a configured single-byte encoding such as ISO-8859-1. This is the best-fit conversion described by the WorstFit research.

This issue affects Apache log4net: from 1.2.9 before 3.6.0.

Users are recommended to upgrade to version 3.6.0, which fixes the issue.

Improper Neutralization of Null Byte or NUL Character vulnerability in the AdoNetAppender of Apache log4net.

Text parameters were bound unchanged, so a NUL character or an unpaired UTF-16 surrogate reached the database as it was. A database that refuses such a value, such as PostgreSQL, rejected the insert and the event was lost; only the first such loss per appender was reported. A party whose data reaches a log message could suppress that event.

This issue affects Apache log4net: from 1.2.9 before 3.6.0.

Users are recommended to upgrade to version 3.6.0, which fixes the issue.

PHP-CGI out-of-bounds read and write during PATH_INFO correction.

The PHP CGI binary (php-cgi), in CGI and FastCGI mode with cgi.fix_pathinfo enabled (the default), can perform an out-of-bounds read and write when the path removed from SCRIPT_FILENAME or PATH_TRANSLATED is longer than the supplied PATH_INFO, or when PATH_INFO is empty. This requires a web server mapping that passes such inconsistent values, or a FastCGI listener reachable by untrusted clients. An unauthenticated remote attacker can crash the process, may obtain process memory if the application exposes PATH_INFO or PATH_TRANSLATED, and may corrupt memory. PHP-FPM and the Apache module are not affected.

This issue affects PHP versions before 8.2.36, 8.3.* before 8.3.37, 8.4.* before 8.4.28 and 8.5.* before 8.5.13.

EdgeChat 2.5.0 through 2.21.0 contains a cross-site scripting vulnerability that allows invited users to inject HTML through unescaped usernames in the Vditor @-mention autocomplete. Attackers can register with a username containing an img onerror payload that executes when mentioned, stealing the localStorage session token to take over victim accounts.

In Eclipse Ditto versions 2.0.0 to 3.8.14 and 3.9.0 to 3.9.8, the authorization check for JSON merge patch commands on Things (HTTP `PATCH` / Ditto Protocol `merge`) does not check permissions for fields

  deleted or set to an empty object by the patch: fields with a `null` value or an empty object value (`{}`) are skipped by the check, and Ditto's regex-based key deletion with the documented `{{
  ~<regex>~ }}` syntax is not recognized as a deletion. An authenticated user with WRITE permission on any part of a Thing can therefore delete other attributes, features and the definition of that Thing,
  or overwrite or create fields as empty objects, including parts the policy revokes or never grants WRITE on.
  
  -->

In Eclipse Ditto versions 2.4.0 to 3.9.8, Thing fields a requester is not allowed to read can be disclosed through the `condition` and `live-channel-condition` headers, which are evaluated against the

  full Thing: the READ check of `live-channel-condition` is skipped when a `condition` header is also present on Thing query commands (3.0.0 to 3.9.8); both headers are evaluated without any authorization
  on WoT Thing Description requests (`Accept: application/td+json`) when WoT TD permission filtering is not active (by default in 3.0.0 to 3.8.14, in 2.4.x with WoT integration enabled, and in 3.9.x with
  filtering disabled); the `condition` of live messages and live events is evaluated without a READ check, and of claim messages without any permission (3.1.0 to 3.9.8); and the twin response of a Thing
  query with a non-matching `live-channel-condition` is returned without filtering it by the policy (3.0.0 to 3.9.8). This allows an authenticated user to read Thing fields they are not allowed to read, in
  some cases without any permission on the Thing.

In Eclipse Ditto versions before 3.8.15 and 3.9.0 to 3.9.8, the policy enforcers do not let a revoke win over a grant in two kinds of permission checks. Checks of several permissions at once compare the highest grant weight with the highest revoke weight across all requested permissions instead of per permission, so the "check permissions" API (`POST /api/2/checkPermissions`, available since 3.7.0) can report a set of permissions as granted although one of them is revoked. Partial permission checks, which authorize retrieving Things and Policies and determine the receivers of events, count a grant on a sub-resource although the same permission is revoked on that sub-resource for another subject of the same authorization context (or, with the memory-optimized policy evaluator, for the same subject). A requester can thereby learn about the existence of Things and Policies and receive metadata without any readable content, and an application relying on the check permissions result may grant access the policy denies. The content of retrieved Things and Policies is still filtered correctly, and modifications are not affected.

In Eclipse Mosquitto versions 2.1.0 to 2.1.2, a broker with a listener that is configured to use the PROXY protocol v2 is vulnerable to an untrusted proxy providing details that cause the broker to accept fake SSL information.



This can be mitigated by following the documented requirements for PROXY listeners: It is very important that only trusted proxies are allowed to connect to any listener using the PROXY protocol, and that clients are not allowed to connect to the listener at all.

A stack-based buffer overflow in an unauthenticated CGI handler of the
Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA Series controller allows remote attackers to send specially
crafted HTTP/S POST requests, leading to memory corruption, webserver restart
and hypothetically potential arbitrary code execution with webserver privileges.
Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.

In Eclipse Ditto versions 3.9.0 to 3.9.8, the resolved policy view (`GET /api/2/policies/{policyId}?policy-view=resolved`) does not restrict merged policy content to what the caller may read in the policy it originates from. Imported and namespace-root entries are returned in full as soon as the caller may read any part of them in the source policy, entries of transitive imports and of the imports of namespace-root policies are only checked against the intermediate policy, and content copied into an entry by `references`, also from another entry of the same policy, is not checked against the referenced entry. An authenticated caller with READ on a policy can therefore read subjects, resources and granted/revoked permissions of policy entries that are hidden from them, including by explicit revokes, when reading the originating policy directly.

The MongoDB Rust Driver does not neutralize NUL characters in the user name and password values it places into the message it builds for SASL PLAIN authentication. A party who can choose the login values that an application passes to the driver can alter where the fields of that message begin and end. This may result in a receiving system reading a login name and secret that differ from the values the application supplied. Authenticating as a different account still requires that account's password. Only deployments that use SASL PLAIN authentication are affected.

The MongoDB Ruby driver can include unmasked connection string content in the error it raises when a connection string cannot be parsed. If that connection string carries a secret, the secret may be disclosed in cleartext through the application's error output or logs. No privileges on the driver and no network access are needed to produce the error; a party able to read the application's error output may obtain the secret.

The MongoDB Ruby Driver does not neutralize NUL characters in the user name and password values it places into the message it builds for SASL PLAIN authentication. A party who can choose the login values that an application passes to the driver can alter where the fields of that message begin and end. This may result in a receiving system reading a login name and secret that differ from the values the application supplied. Authenticating as a different account still requires that account's password. Only deployments that use SASL PLAIN authentication are affected.

The MongoDB Python Driver does not neutralize NUL characters in the user name and password values it places into the message it builds for SASL PLAIN authentication. A party who can choose the login values that an application passes to the driver can alter where the fields of that message begin and end. This may result in a receiving system reading a login name and secret that differ from the values the application supplied. Authenticating as a different account still requires that account's password. Only deployments that use SASL PLAIN authentication are affected.

A credential-handling weakness in the MongoDB Python Driver allows a configuration option value that protects private key material to be written in clear text into the embedding application's own output and log records when a driver object is converted to text. A party able to read that output may obtain the credential. Obtaining it requires read access to the application's local output or log files.

The MongoDB PHP extension includes the full connection string it was given in the error it raises when that string cannot be parsed. A party able to influence any part of the connection string, including a part that holds no secret, can cause the resulting message to carry credentials into the application's standard error output and log files. This may result in unintended disclosure of authentication material to anyone able to read that output.

The MongoDB Node.js Driver does not neutralize NUL characters in the user name and password values it places into the message it builds for SASL PLAIN authentication. A party who can choose the login values that an application passes to the driver can alter where the fields of that message begin and end. This may result in a receiving system reading a login name and secret that differ from the values the application supplied. Authenticating as a different account still requires that account's password. Only deployments that use SASL PLAIN authentication are affected.

A weakness in the MongoDB Node.js driver can place sensitive information taken from an application-supplied connection string into the text of an error produced while that connection string is being parsed. The error is generated inside the application process before any database connection is made, so no database account and no network access are needed for it to occur. A party able to read the application's error output or log files may thereby obtain database credentials that the application's configuration source would otherwise keep to a narrower audience.

A component of the MongoDB Java Driver that processes connection configuration places credential values taken from that configuration into generated text and error output without replacing them with a placeholder, unlike other parts of the driver. A party able to read output produced by an application that embeds the driver may obtain database or proxy credentials in clear text.

The MongoDB Java driver applies its DNS seedlist domain restriction to a record value that is later re-interpreted differently when the connection target is parsed, so the name that is checked and the name that is used can differ. An unauthenticated party who can set or forge the DNS service record for the seed domain in a connection string can cause the driver to direct its session to an unrelated host and to complete certificate verification against that host instead. This may result in unintended disclosure of application data and of configured database credentials, and in unintended content being returned to the application as query results.

The MongoDB Java Driver does not neutralize NUL characters in the user name and password values it places into the message it builds for SASL PLAIN authentication. A party who can choose the login values that an application passes to the driver can alter where the fields of that message begin and end. This may result in a receiving system reading a login name and secret that differ from the values the application supplied. Authenticating as a different account still requires that account's password. Only deployments that use SASL PLAIN authentication are affected.

The MongoDB Go driver's connection string parser includes the raw, undecoded value of a query option in the error it returns when that value contains invalid percent encodings. When the option holds a secret, such as a TLS key file password or an AWS session token, the secret appears in plain text in the error. A party with low-privileged read access to wherever the application records or displays that error may learn the secret.

The MongoDB Go Driver does not neutralize NUL characters in the user name and password values it places into the message it builds for SASL PLAIN authentication. A party who can choose the login values that an application passes to the driver can alter where the fields of that message begin and end. This may result in a receiving system reading a login name and secret that differ from the values the application supplied. Authenticating as a different account still requires that account's password. Only deployments that use SASL PLAIN authentication are affected.

A MongoDB C# Driver component that interprets connection configuration supplied by the hosting application can include the caller-supplied configuration value in the text of the error it raises when that value cannot be interpreted. The redaction applied to that text does not cover all forms in which secret material may appear, so authentication material embedded in the configuration value can be preserved in the resulting error text and in anything that records it. Exploitation requires only the low privilege needed to observe the application's own error output or logs on the system where the driver runs; no database credentials or server connectivity are required. The result is disclosure of sensitive information to parties whose access to error output is broader than their intended access to the configuration secret.

The MongoDB C# Driver does not neutralize NUL characters in the user name and password values it places into the message it builds for SASL PLAIN authentication. A party who can choose the login values that an application passes to the driver can alter where the fields of that message begin and end. This may result in a receiving system reading a login name and secret that differ from the values the application supplied. Authenticating as a different account still requires that account's password. Only deployments that use SASL PLAIN authentication are affected.

An improper neutralization of delimiters in the MongoDB C# driver's DNS SRV connection-string resolution lets an unauthenticated party who can answer the client's DNS SRV query place a host outside the trusted domain into the client's server list. When an application resolves the connection string through the affected API and connects with the result, application data, authentication credentials and query results may pass through that host. This may result in unintended disclosure of data and credentials and in forged query results.

The MongoDB C Driver places a submitted connection-string option value into a diagnostic message without redaction when that option fails validation. The message is returned to the calling application and is also written to the process's standard error by the driver's default logging behavior. A party that can influence the connection string given to an application using the driver may cause that field's contents to be recorded, which may result in unintended disclosure of information the application placed in that field.

A buffer overflow vulnerability exists in the SNMP service of the Ethernet Remote I/Os products. An unauthenticated remote attacker could exploit improper handling of specially crafted SNMP requests, potentially leading to a denial-of-service condition on the affected device.

A buffer overflow vulnerability exists in the web management service of the Ethernet Remote I/Os products. An unauthenticated remote attacker could exploit insufficient bounds checking of specially crafted HTTP requests, potentially causing the web management service to crash and resulting in a denial-of-service condition.

Dokploy is a free, self-hostable Platform as a Service (PaaS). Prior to 0.31.1, a user-controlled schedule appName is joined into the schedule directory path and interpolated without shell quoting into commands that create the directory and write the schedule script. An authenticated user who can create or update a dokploy-server schedule can inject operating-system commands that execute with the Dokploy process privileges when the schedule is saved, including root privileges on typical installations. This issue is fixed in version 0.31.1.

Dokploy is a free, self-hostable Platform as a Service (PaaS). Prior to 0.31.1, the Nixpacks publishDirectory build setting accepts shell metacharacters and is interpolated into a docker cp command executed through child_process.exec. An authenticated user with access to an application can execute arbitrary commands on the Dokploy host when triggering a Nixpacks deployment, leading to host compromise through the privileged Docker environment. This issue is fixed in version 0.31.1.

The Chatterbug Forms – Fast, Flexible WordPress Form Builder plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to arbitrary file deletion due to insufficient file path validation in the cbforms_delete_uploaded_files function in all versions up to, and including, 1.1 This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to delete arbitrary files on the server, which can easily lead to remote code execution when the right file is deleted (such as wp-config.php). Exploitation requires an administrator to delete the attacker-planted form entry, and the attacker must know or be able to guess the absolute path of a file writable by the PHP process. Successful exploitation additionally requires an action by an administrator — the attacker cannot trigger the vulnerability on their own.

The Recipe Card Blocks Lite plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to authorization bypass in all versions up to, and including, 4.0.1. This is due to the plugin not properly verifying that a user is authorized to perform an action. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with contributor-level access and above, to overwrite the stored post_content of any post or page on the site, including published posts and private drafts authored by administrators or other users.

The VidShop for WooCommerce plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Sensitive Information Exposure in versions up to, and including, 1.10.0 via the /vsfw/v1/products/{id} REST API endpoint. This is due to the endpoint's permission_callback (check_public_permission) returning true unconditionally and the get_item() handler only checking that the product and video exist — it does not check the product's post_status or catalog visibility, nor does it verify that the product is actually linked to the supplied video_id. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to enumerate product IDs and read private, draft, and catalog-hidden WooCommerce products' names, short descriptions, prices, variations, attributes, and stock information that would otherwise be hidden from public view.

Okta Privileged Access (OPA) Gateway includes a version of the FreeRDP library affected by memory management issues in its smartcard redirection handling. When an RDP session is established meeting specific session criteria, command execution within the context of the local Gateway service account may be allowed.

The Okta Client SDK for Python (okta-client-python) includes client authentication values (client_secret or JWT assertions) as query parameters in the front-channel authorization URL when executing the authorization code flow without Pushed Authorization Requests (PAR). When PAR is disabled, unsupported by the authorization server, or fails, the SDK falls back to standard authorization URL construction, transmitting these parameters via user-agent requests.

RepoManager is a self-hosted deb/rpm package repository. Prior to 5.13.3, an attacker who controls an upstream RPM repository mirrored by a RepoManager instance can provide a package filename through the primary.xml <location href> field; the mirror passes that filename into a shell-interpreted RPM query, allowing shell metacharacters to execute commands as the www-data service account. The target must mirror an upstream repository controlled by the attacker, and the default "Check GPG signatures" option triggers the vulnerable call. The command executes before a later signature-verification failure, so a valid signed package is not required. Fixed in 5.13.3.

RepoManager is a self-hosted deb/rpm package repository. Prior to 5.13.3, the authenticated get-unit-log action accepts a caller-controlled logfile value. Validate::string() escapes HTML but leaves path traversal components unchanged. The action joins the caller-controlled logfile to SERVICE_LOGS_DIR without enforcing containment, so traversal can resolve the file read outside that directory. www/controllers/ajax/status/service.php reads and returns the resolved file, and any authenticated user can invoke the action to retrieve files readable by the www-data service account, including application configuration, source code, and the GPG signing-key passphrase. Fixed in 5.13.3.

RepoManager is a self-hosted deb/rpm package repository. Prior to 5.13.3, an authenticated user can supply a user-controlled, array-valued GPG key identifier to the key deletion action. Validate::string() filters HTML characters but not shell metacharacters. The user-controlled identifier reaches the delete action without shell-safe encoding. controllers/Gpg.php contains the vulnerable deletion path. Process::execute() passes the command string through proc_open() and /bin/sh -c, allowing the attacker to execute arbitrary OS commands as the web/PHP process. This can expose secrets or poison packages. Authentication is required, but the advisory makes an administrator-only restriction conditional on the intended access policy and does not establish an administrator role as a prerequisite. Fixed in 5.13.3.

Tamari is a fully-featured recipe manager web application built using Python and the Flask Framework. Prior to 1.7.2, an authenticated user can bypass the recipe-autofill SSRF check by submitting a hostname under the user's control through the Autofill from URL feature; the hostname can resolve to a public address during validation and a private or internal address during the later connection. In app/myrecipes/routes.py, is_safe_autofill_url validates the first DNS response, but recipe autofill passes the original URL to requests.get, which independently resolves the hostname and can connect to the internal address. The fetched response is parsed into recipe fields, enabling internal-service reconnaissance and potential data exposure; no redirect is required, and disabling redirects does not stop this DNS-rebinding bypass. This issue is fixed in 1.7.2.

Collabora Online is a collaborative online office suite based on LibreOffice technology. Prior to 24.04.19.3, 25.04.13.3, and 26.04.3.3, the RouteToken query parameter is reflected into the unauthenticated admin-console page without HTML encoding. The admin-console page is served without authentication. A victim must load a crafted URL, and token exposure requires the victim to be an administrator already signed in to the console; the reflected value can run script in the Collabora Online origin and expose the console authentication token. This issue is fixed in versions 24.04.19.3, 25.04.13.3, and 26.04.3.3.

aMQTT is an open source MQTT broker and client. From 0.11.0 until 0.12.1, the QoS 2 transaction handler in amqtt/mqtt/protocol/handler.py, _handle_qos2_message_flow(), can retain transaction state and packet identifiers when a client disconnects before the handshake completes, unlike QoS 1 flows that expire after the default five-second timeout. A remote client can repeatedly begin QoS 2 flows and disconnect without maintaining long-lived connections; anonymous clients can do this with the default configuration, while authenticated deployments remain affected when a client may initiate QoS 2 flows. The retained state grows broker memory until resource exhaustion can terminate the process; no confidentiality or integrity impact is identified. This issue is fixed in version 0.12.1.

The Okta .NET SDK Abstractions library systematically writes per-request authentication credentials to a shared HTTP client instance, rather than being isolated to individual outbound request objects. When using scoped child clients, a subsequent scoped request can overwrite the shared client configuration. Because the original parent client credential has not been restored, subsequent outbound requests may be transmitted using the newly written credential, which can result in subsequent actions being executed under the context of an incorrect security principal in the Okta Management API and improper attribution in audit logs.

The Okta .NET SDK Abstractions library improperly synchronizes authentication credentials set on a shared HTTP client during request execution. When concurrent requests are dispatched for different principals, one principal's credential may be transmitted on an outbound request intended for another principal, which can result in credential exposure and lead to unauthorized actions performed as the affected principal at the Okta Management API.

The Okta Swift Management SDK does not percent-encode forward slash (/) characters during path parameter interpolation. If an application supplies input containing relative path sequences (e.g., ../) to an SDK method, standard URL normalization may direct the outbound request to an alternative Okta Management API endpoint.

In the Okta .NET SDK Abstractions library, outbound HTTP requests are not restricted to the configured Okta organization domain when processing certain URL formats. If a URL parameter is modified to specify an external host, the library may transmit the configured SSWS API token to that unintended destination.

In the Auth0 Authorization Extension, request authentication handling can process claims from query parameters independently of header validation. Under specific preconditions, this may allow an authenticated tenant user to issue requests to the extension's administrative endpoints. Also, input handling during rule generation may permit modification of the tenant login rule published by the extension.

The EU Order Withdrawal Button for WooCommerce plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via the 'HTTP_USER_AGENT' parameter in all versions up to, and including, 2.4.6 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses an injected page. Execution requires an Administrator or Shop Manager to open the Withdrawals Preview modal and click the injected note element, which the attacker can enlarge via a retained style attribute to cover the entire note area. Successful exploitation additionally requires an action by an administrator — the attacker cannot trigger the vulnerability on their own.

In Eclipse versions 1.5-1.6.13, 2.0.0-2.0.22 and 2.1.0-2.1.2, the client library libmosquitto does not reject Will messages with payloads greater than 65535 bytes when calling `mosquitto_will_set()` or `mosquitto_will_set_v5()`. This results in up to 65535 bytes of uninitialised heap memory being transmitted as the Will.



This can be mitigated by only passing payloads with a maximum length of 65535 bytes.

A hard-coded cryptographic key vulnerability exists in affected Ethernet swiches. The use of a shared cryptographic key with insufficient key strength could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker, under certain conditions, to impersonate affected devices and potentially compromise the confidentiality and integrity of communications.

An improper firmware authenticity verification vulnerability exists in the affected Ethernet Switches products. An authenticated remote attacker with administrative privileges could exploit the lack of cryptographic signature verification to install unauthorized firmware, potentially leading to arbitrary code execution on the affected device.

GPAC before 26.02.0 contains an out-of-bounds read vulnerability in m2tsdmx_send_packet() in src/filters/dmx_m2ts.c caused by double-skipping the VC-1 start-code offset. Attackers can supply a crafted MPEG-2 TS VC-1 stream that underflows the remaining length, causing memcpy() to over-read and crash MP4Box on import.

GPAC before 26.07.0 contains a heap-based buffer overflow in gf_mpd_resolve_url() in src/media_tools/mpd.c that allows attackers to write past a heap buffer via crafted DASH manifests. Attackers can supply a crafted MPD whose segment template expands beyond the allocation through unchecked strcat() calls, crashing MP4Box and causing denial of service.

GPAC before 26.07.0 contains an uncontrolled recursion vulnerability in dasher_gather_deps() in src/filters/dasher.c that fails to detect cyclic stream dependency chains. Attackers can supply a crafted MPEG-2 TS file that MP4Box processes with -dash, exhausting the stack and crashing the process for denial of service.

@fastify/http-proxy is a Fastify plugin that proxies HTTP and WebSocket traffic to an upstream server. In versions from 9.0.0 up to but not including 11.6.10, when the plugin is registered with websocket support enabled, a WebSocket upgrade that is pipelined behind another HTTP request on the same cleartext connection arrives while that request's response is still attached to the socket. The shared upgrade listener sees the socket is already claimed and returns early without taking the upgrade, but it does not attach an error listener to the raw socket, and Node.js has already removed its own error listener before emitting the upgrade event. A later socket error on that connection, such as a client connection reset, is therefore unhandled and terminates the Node.js process. A single unauthenticated connection that pipelines an upgrade behind a normal request and then resets is enough to crash the server, and it can be repeated to keep the process down. Upgrades over TLS are not affected. The issue is fixed in @fastify/http-proxy 11.6.10, and users should upgrade to 11.6.10 or later.

ImageMagick before 7.1.2-35 contains a use after free vulnerability in the MSL decoder that can be triggered when processing crafted MSL image files. Attackers can supply a specially crafted MSL image to cause memory corruption, potentially crashing the application or leading to further compromise.

ImageMagick before 7.1.2-35 contains a code injection vulnerability in the MAGICK, XBM, XPM and UIL encoders that allows local attackers to inject content via crafted filenames. Attackers with access to the output directory and control over the filename can inject additional headers or code into the generated image source output.

ImageMagick before 7.1.2-35 contains a heap buffer overflow vulnerability that allows attackers to write beyond allocated heap memory by supplying crafted images. Attackers can provide a crafted set of images processed by the magick stream operation to corrupt heap memory and crash the application.

ImageMagick before 7.1.2-35 contains a use after free vulnerability in the EXR decoder that is triggered when a specific memory allocation fails. Attackers can supply crafted EXR images processed under memory pressure to trigger the use after free, causing crashes or memory corruption.

ImageMagick before 7.1.2-35 contains a policy bypass vulnerability that allows attackers to evade resource limits because a policy check is missing when reading XMP profiles. Attackers can supply an image with a crafted XMP profile to trigger excessive memory usage and cause denial of service.

ImageMagick before 7.1.2-35 contains a heap buffer over-read vulnerability in the TIFF decoder that allows attackers to corrupt heap memory by supplying a crafted TIFF image. Attackers can provide a malicious TIFF file that, when encoded in a specific output format, triggers a heap buffer over-write causing memory corruption.

ImageMagick before 7.1.2-35 contains a double free vulnerability that allows attackers to trigger an invalid memory free by using the DPC compare metric. Attackers can supply images for comparison with the DPC metric to corrupt memory and crash the application, causing denial of service.

ImageMagick before 7.1.2-35 contains a null pointer dereference vulnerability that allows attackers to crash the process by using the -subimage option on a single-image list. Attackers can supply input producing an image list with only one image while -subimage is applied, causing a denial of service.

ImageMagick before 7.1.2-35 contains a heap buffer over-read vulnerability that allows attackers to read beyond allocated memory when BGRO image data is imported. Attackers can supply crafted BGRO data for processing to crash the application or leak adjacent heap memory contents.

NocoDB before 2026.10.1 contains a stored CSS injection vulnerability that allows authenticated Commenter or Editor users to inject inline styles by placing single quotes in mention text. Attackers can break out of the single-quoted data-id attribute in comments or rich text cells to overlay or rearrange the interface for other viewers.

NocoDB before 2026.10.1 contains a stored HTML injection vulnerability that allows authenticated users with record edit rights to inject forms, images, and styled overlays into rich text cells, which are sanitized only with DOMPurify's default policy. Attackers can place a page-sized spoofed sign-in form or remote image in a cell to harvest passwords and disclose viewer IP addresses in expanded records, gallery and kanban cards, and shared views.

NocoDB before 2026.10.0 contains an sql injection vulnerability that allows authenticated users with the Creator role to inject SQL by supplying a crafted formula parsed_tree during table creation. Attackers can set a malicious binary-expression operator that is interpolated into a knex.raw fragment, reading user and token tables and escalating to super administrator on SQLite installs.

NocoDB before 2026.10.1 contains an incorrect authorization vulnerability that allows organization Creators to reach routes restricted to other roles because the aclFn middleware never enforced allowedRoles. Attackers can generate a super admin password reset link via org-users endpoints to take over the instance, or read and modify SSO client secrets.

NocoDB before 2026.10.1 contains an information disclosure vulnerability that allows unauthenticated attackers to download data exports by reconstructing predictable file paths under nc/uploads/data-export. Attackers can derive paths from the table id, base, table and view titles, and export time to read full exports, including fields hidden from public shared views.

NocoDB before 2026.10.1 contains a template injection vulnerability that allows authenticated Creator-role users to execute server-side JavaScript by supplying array-form property paths to Handlebars helpers in webhook templates. Attackers can bypass the string-only prototype guard to reach the function constructor, running operating-system commands with server privileges or exfiltrating process-internal values via outbound requests.

NocoDB from 0.253.0 before 2026.09.1 contains an incorrect authorization vulnerability in baseUserDelete that allows base Creators to remove higher-privileged Owners due to a broken role power comparison. Attackers holding the Creator role can remove other Owners of a base, since getProjectRolePower returns -1 for the target and never refuses the request.

NocoDB from 2026.07.0 before 2026.10.0 contains an sql injection vulnerability that allows users with Creator role to inject SQL through unescaped backslashes in the DATETIME_FORMAT formula format argument on MySQL-backed bases. Attackers can place a backslash before a quote to terminate the DATE_FORMAT string literal and read any data reachable by the data source's database user, including tables outside the base.

NocoDB before 2026.10.1 contains an authentication bypass vulnerability that allows holders of revoked OAuth access tokens to authenticate as first-party sessions by presenting them through the session header. Attackers can bypass revocation, client-existence, route allowlist and granted_resources scope checks to modify victim profiles, upload to storage, and force global sign-outs.

NocoDB before 2026.10.1 contains a credential exposure vulnerability in the connection-test endpoint that allows authorized integration users to redirect stored credentials by overriding connection host, port, and user fields. Attackers can point the test at a server they control to capture offline-crackable PostgreSQL md5 or MySQL handshakes and recover the stored database password.

NocoDB from 0.301.4 before 2026.10.0 contains an information disclosure vulnerability that allows authenticated workspace viewers to read pending invitation tokens through the workspace member list. Attackers can redeem an exposed higher-privileged invitation token at signup to claim the invited account and escalate to roles such as workspace owner.

NocoDB before 2026.10.1 contains a consent phishing vulnerability that allows unauthenticated attackers to register OAuth clients with arbitrary HTTPS redirect URIs through the unauthenticated dynamic client registration endpoint. Attackers can impersonate trusted applications on a consent screen lacking unverified-client warnings or redirect host display, obtaining tokens to read and write victim tables and records.

NocoDB before 2026.10.1 contains an SQL injection vulnerability because select-field option titles are embedded into MySQL or MariaDB enum/set column definitions with only single-quote doubling, leaving backslashes unescaped. A base creator or owner can end an option title with a backslash to escape the literal and append ALTER TABLE clauses, adding, dropping or renaming columns and altering indexes in the connected database.

NocoDB before 2026.10.0 contains an account takeover vulnerability that allows users with the base creator role to hijack other accounts by resending base invitations. Attackers can trigger baseUserInviteResend to mint a new invite_token, read it from the base member list, and reset the victim's password through signup, taking over owner or super admin accounts.

NocoDB before 2026.10.0 contains an information disclosure vulnerability that allows unauthenticated attackers to read hidden columns by supplying comma-separated group-by column lists. Attackers with a shared view link can pair a visible and hidden column to bypass restrictSharedViewColumnReferences and retrieve hidden values tied to individual rows.

NocoDB before 2026.10.0 contains an improper access control vulnerability that allows Creator-role users to attach NocoDB's internal database by supplying is_meta and is_local flags. Attackers can create sources or bases with these flags to expose user, token and integration tables, then read and modify records including user roles.

NocoDB before 2026.10.1 contains an information disclosure vulnerability that allows unauthenticated shared view link holders to read hidden columns by grouping on physical column names. Attackers can supply a hidden column's physical name or the unchecked sub-group parameter to the public group-by endpoint to reveal hidden values, counts, and column existence.

NocoDB before 2026.09.0 contains an sql injection vulnerability that allows authenticated Creator or Owner users to inject raw SQL by persisting a crafted formula parsed_tree reused without revalidation. Attackers can bypass the SQLite metadata path guard with an alias to plant the tree, escalating to super administrator or executing OS commands on external PostgreSQL hosts.

NocoDB from 0.301.4 before 2026.10.1 writes the nc_token session cookie from script in the Enterprise useGlobal composable without the Secure attribute. Network-positioned attackers can observe or induce plain-HTTP requests to https instances to capture the session token and impersonate the victim until expiry.

NocoDB before 2026.09.0 contains an improper authorization vulnerability that allows workspace Creator users to read plaintext notification webhook URLs by querying the webhook plugin listing endpoint. Attackers can replay exposed Slack, Teams, Discord and Mattermost webhook URLs directly against messaging providers to post arbitrary messages into organization chat channels.

NocoDB before 2026.09.0 contains a server-side template injection vulnerability that allows authenticated Creator or Owner users to execute JavaScript by abusing Handlebars webhook helpers. Attackers can supply property paths like constructor.constructor to pluck, sortBy, filter, or withSort helpers to reach the Function constructor and run operating-system commands.

NocoDB before 2026.09.0 contains a missing authorization vulnerability in the job status polling endpoint of jobs.controller.ts that lacks an @Acl decorator. Unauthenticated attackers with a job id can read buffered status messages and completion payloads, exposing signed export download URLs or new base identifiers.

NocoDB before 2026.09.0 contains an authorization bypass vulnerability in extract-ids.middleware.ts that allows authenticated users to resolve roles against another base by supplying an MCP token id in the query string. Attackers with Viewer access on one base can mint an MCP token and pass its id to read another base's metadata, including table lists and member email addresses.

NocoDB before 2026.08.1 contains an authorization bypass vulnerability that allows authenticated Creators to access another tenant's external database by reusing a victim source id when adding a source. Because NcConnectionMgrv2 caches connections by bare source id, attackers can reflect the victim's cached database schema and read, update, and insert records through their own base models.

NocoDB before 2026.10.1 contains a user enumeration vulnerability that allows unauthenticated attackers to identify pending invitees through a distinct sign-in error message. Attackers can submit sign-in requests where validateUser in auth.service.ts skips password comparison for saltless invited accounts, confirming the email address has an account.

NocoDB before 2026.10.1 contains a user enumeration vulnerability that allows unauthenticated attackers to determine registered email addresses by observing differing sign-up endpoint responses. Attackers can submit addresses to signup in users.service.ts and compare error messages to identify existing accounts and pending Enterprise invitations, even under invite-only signup.

NocoDB before 2026.08.0 contains an sql injection vulnerability that allows authenticated Creator or Owner users to execute database functions by supplying zero-argument function calls as column default values. Attackers can plant functions like version() or inet_server_addr() in PostgreSQL or MySQL column definitions and read results through record APIs, disclosing server addresses, role names, and engine details.

NocoDB before 2026.08.0 contains a stored cross-site scripting vulnerability that allows authenticated Creator or Editor users to execute script by injecting markup into fields rendered through URL() formulas. The canvas grid renderer assigns unsanitized formula output to innerHTML, letting attackers steal session tokens from localStorage and take over accounts of users viewing the table.

NocoDB before 2026.04.1 fails to clear reset_password_token and reset_password_expires in users.service.ts when a password is changed, leaving earlier reset links valid. Attackers holding an unexpired reset link, such as from prior mailbox access, can set a new password and regain control of the account.

NocoDB before 2026.08.0 contains an authorization bypass vulnerability that allows anonymous share link holders to access records excluded by a shared view's row filter, because the read-by-primary-key path ignores the view's filters. Attackers can request the public attachment-download or nested-link listing routes with a record id to mint signed download URLs for hidden files and read linked-record data.

NocoDB before 2026.08.0 contains an information disclosure vulnerability that allows unauthenticated shared-base link holders to read the base's stored plaintext password through the general base metadata endpoint. Attackers with a share link can query the base read or list responses in bases.controller.ts, which skip password stripping in sanitizeBase.ts, to obtain reusable plaintext passwords.

NocoDB before 2026.08.0 contains an insecure direct object reference vulnerability that allows unauthenticated attackers to access records hidden by a shared view's row filter by supplying arbitrary primary keys. Attackers with the share link can request attachment downloads and many-to-many or has-many link listings for excluded records to obtain their attachment files and linked record identities.

NocoDB from 2026.06.2 before 2026.08.0 contains an authorization bypass vulnerability that allows authenticated base Editors to write to data-read-only sources by abusing the internal batch endpoint. NocoDB before 2026.08.0 contains an authorization bypass in shared-view relation endpoints because parent-record lookups apply only the primary key, not the view's row filter. Anonymous share-link holders can enumerate auto-increment primary keys against the has-many, many-to-many, one-to-many and link-to-another-record routes to read linked records of filtered-out rows.

NocoDB before 2026.08.0 contains an information disclosure vulnerability that allows unauthenticated attackers to access attachments of filtered-out records through the shared view attachment-download endpoint. Attackers holding a public share link can enumerate sequential primary keys to obtain signed download paths for files on records the view's row filter excludes.

NocoDB before 2026.08.0 contains a server-side request forgery vulnerability that allows authenticated base Editors to make backend HTTP requests by supplying arbitrary URLs to the integration remote fetch operation. Attackers can control the method, headers, and body to reach internal APIs, loopback services, and cloud metadata endpoints, reading responses and echoed decrypted integration secrets.

NocoDB before 2026.10.0 contains an insecure direct object reference vulnerability that allows authenticated users to obtain signed download URLs for other bases' attachments by storing foreign attachment paths in their own rows via prepareNocoData. Attackers with write access to an attachment column can have _convertAttachmentType or the attachment download endpoint sign the foreign path, reading cross-base files despite secure attachment mode.

NocoDB before 2026.07.0 contains an SQL injection vulnerability in its MySQL and SQLite clients that inserts the column precision value into generated data-definition statements without numeric validation. Authenticated users with the Creator or Owner base role can supply a crafted precision value when creating or updating a column to close the type declaration and execute arbitrary SQL against the base's data source.

NocoDB before 2026.08.0 contains an authorization bypass vulnerability in public shared-view endpoints that fetch records by primary key without applying the view's row filter. Anonymous share link holders can enumerate sequential primary keys on link, has-many, and attachment download endpoints to read excluded records' linked data and download their attachments.

NocoDB before 2026.08.0 contains a stored cross-site scripting vulnerability that allows any authenticated user to register OAuth clients with javascript: redirect URIs. NocoDB before 2026.10.1 contains an authentication bypass vulnerability that allows OAuth token holders to act as full sessions because OAuth access tokens are signed with the instance JWT secret. Attackers can present a narrowly scoped OAuth token to the session strategy, short-lived-token exchange, or NocoSocket handshake to gain the granting user's full privileges.

NocoDB before 2026.05.3 contains an account takeover vulnerability that allows invited users to complete other invitees' signups because batch invitations share one token across all recipients. Attackers holding a valid batch invite can submit another invitee's email with the shared non-expiring token to set its password and take over that account, including higher-role ones.

OpenWrt LuCI luci-app-travelmate on master before 3.0.0-1, on openwrt-25.12 before 2.4.9-6, and on openwrt-24.10 and openwrt-23.05 (no fix available) grants file exec permissions for state-mutating commands in the read scope of its rpcd ACL, letting authenticated read-only users run those commands as root. Attackers can invoke ubus file exec on /etc/init.d/travelmate setup, start, stop, restart, or /sbin/ifup to modify and commit network and firewall configuration or disrupt the travelmate daemon.

@fastify/static is the Fastify plugin for serving static files. In versions up to and including 10.1.11, when it is configured to deny or ignore dotfiles together with directory listing enabled, a request for a denied dot-directory returns its directory listing instead of being refused. The underlying send step answers with a forbidden response, but the listing fallback misreads that response on a path ending in a slash as a directory without an index file and serves the listing anyway. An unauthenticated client can enumerate the names of files and subdirectories, recursively, inside dot-directories the operator explicitly denied, such as version control, backup, and key file names. File contents remain protected and only names are disclosed. The issue is fixed in @fastify/static 10.1.12, and users should upgrade to 10.1.12 or later. As a workaround, disable directory listing or do not serve a root that contains dot-directories.

@fastify/reply-from is a Fastify plugin that forwards requests to an upstream HTTP server. In versions 12.8.1 through 12.8.3, its buildURL function checked the attacker-supplied source string for parent-directory segments, but when the source begins with the same special scheme as the base, such as http or https, the WHATWG URL parser drops the scheme and resolves the remainder as a relative path. A payload that glues the scheme to a percent-encoded parent-directory sequence therefore passes the check, because the inspected segment reads as the scheme plus the dots rather than a bare parent-directory token, while the proxy forwards the encoded traversal unchanged. An upstream that percent-decodes the request path before resolving dot-segments then serves a path outside the configured prefix, so an unauthenticated client scoped to an upstream prefix, or relying on Fastify route guards in front of the proxy, can escape that prefix and reach sibling or parent upstream endpoints. The per-segment check added in 12.8.1 is what the scheme prefix bypasses, and releases up to 12.8.0 already rejected the decoded form. The issue is fixed in @fastify/reply-from 12.8.4, and users should upgrade to 12.8.4 or later.

A flaw was found in nbdkit. The qcow2dec filter's zstd_compressed_cluster() function incorrectly sets the ZSTD input buffer size to the uncompressed cluster size instead of the compressed buffer size. A crafted QCOW2 image with ZSTD-compressed clusters can trigger a heap over-read, leading to a denial of service and potentially exposing heap memory.

A stored XSS in pretix-adyen has been discovered where an attacker could configure his own ticket shop in a way that API calls are not made to Adyen, but an attacker-controlled server. Results of these API calls would then be embedded in a part of the shop without proper escaping, leading to full XSS including potential session takeover.

The fix for CVE-2026-127174 published in 2026.9.2 is incomplete: When expanding an export from "some events" to "all events", it is checked that the acting user is part of a team with permission to all events, but this check is not correctly bound to the organizer and could also be passed through permissions on a different organizer.
A bug caused room permissions to leak into the world permissions of the acting user during certain actions.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.16, a user who does not hold the "admin" or "power" Splunk roles could make unauthorized changes when restoring archived indexed data or cause a Denial of Service (DoS) on the Splunk Enterprise instance.
The vulnerability is possible because the Representational State Transfer (REST) API does not require the indexes_edit capability for archived-data restoration actions.
For more information see Define roles on the Splunk platform with capabilities (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.6/manage-splunk-platform-users-and-roles/define-roles-on-the-splunk-platform-with-capabilities) in the Splunk documentation.
For more information see Restore archived indexed data (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-indexers-and-indexer-clusters/10.6/back-up-and-archive-your-indexes/restore-archived-indexed-data) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.4, 10.2.8, 10.0.11, and 9.4.16, a user who holds the "power" Splunk role could create and share a metric alert that causes Analytics Workspace to run a malicious Search Processing Language (SPL) when another authenticated user opens a link to the alert. The malicious SPL could expose data, modify data, or disrupt services available in the affected session. 
The vulnerability is possible because Analytics Workspace does not fully neutralize metric alert names before including the names in SPL.
The vulnerability requires the attacker to phish the user by tricking them into opening a link that the attacker creates. The user who holds the "power" Splunk role should not be able to exploit the vulnerability at will.
For more information see Alerts in the Analytics Workspace (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/create-dashboards-and-reports/analytics-workspace/10.4/using-the-analytics-workspace/alerts-in-the-analytics-workspace) and Define roles on the Splunk platform with capabilities (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.4/manage-splunk-platform-users-and-roles/define-roles-on-the-splunk-platform-with-capabilities) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.4, 10.2.8, 10.0.11, and 9.4.17, a user that holds a role with the edit_own_objects capability but does not hold the edit_view_html capability could create or modify a private Hypertext Markup Language (HTML) view through the Representational State Transfer (REST) API.
The vulnerability is possible because the REST API applies the edit_own_objects capability when it creates or modifies private HTML-based views instead of requiring the edit_view_html capability.
For more information see Define roles on the Splunk platform with capabilities (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.2/manage-splunk-platform-users-and-roles/define-roles-on-the-splunk-platform-with-capabilities) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17, a user who holds the "power" Splunk role could craft a shared Classic Dashboard that runs arbitrary Search Processing Language (SPL) commands for another authenticated user. Exploitation requires the dashboard viewer to open the shared dashboard. The injected commands could access data available to the dashboard viewer, modify data available to the dashboard viewer, and partially disrupt Splunk Enterprise.
For more information see Add sparklines to search results (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/search/search-manual/10.6/calculate-statistics/add-sparklines-to-search-results), Configure dashboard permissions (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/create-dashboards-and-reports/simple-xml-dashboards/10.6/manage-and-share-dashboards/configure-dashboard-permissions), and SPL safeguards for risky commands (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.6/best-practices-for-splunk-platform-security/spl-safeguards-for-risky-commands) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17, a user who holds the "power" Splunk role could add attacker-controlled Search Processing Language (SPL) to a shared dashboard. When another user opens the dashboard in Splunk Web, Splunk Enterprise could run the attacker-controlled SPL using the permissions of that dashboard viewer. The attacker-controlled SPL could expose stored credentials, modify indexed data, and reduce availability.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk Enterprise does not neutralize special elements in search filter values before it builds optimized search jobs.
The vulnerability requires the attacker to phish the affected user by tricking them into initiating a request within their browser. The attacker should not be able to exploit the vulnerability at will.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17, a user who holds the "power" Splunk role could create and share a dashboard that contains attacker-controlled Search Processing Language (SPL). The SPL could run using the permissions of the user who opens the dashboard. With this access, the user who created the dashboard could expose stored credentials and write data to an index.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk Enterprise does not correctly escape field names in searches that use the rename command.
For more information see rename (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/spl-search-reference/10.4/search-commands/rename) and SPL safeguards for risky commands (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.4/best-practices-for-splunk-platform-security/spl-safeguards-for-risky-commands) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.16, a user who does not hold the "admin" or "power" Splunk roles could use Data Model Acceleration to run malicious Search Processing Language (SPL) commands and perform actions through the Representational State Transfer (REST) API that the user cannot perform directly.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk Enterprise does not neutralize user-provided data before it adds that data to a generated search.
For more information, see Accelerate data models (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/manage-knowledge-objects/knowledge-management-manual/10.2/use-data-summaries-to-accelerate-searches/accelerate-data-models), Define roles on the Splunk platform with capabilities (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.2/manage-splunk-platform-users-and-roles/define-roles-on-the-splunk-platform-with-capabilities), and About the search language (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/search/search-manual/10.6/search-overview/about-the-search-language).

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17, a user who holds the "power" Splunk role could store malicious Search Processing Language (SPL) in a shared dashboard. The malicious SPL could run using the permissions of the user who opened the dashboard and could access or modify data available to that user and disrupt Splunk Enterprise availability.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk Enterprise does not preserve quoted search argument boundaries when it processes a dashboard search.
The vulnerability requires the attacker to phish the affected user by tricking them into initiating a request within their browser. The attacker, a user who holds the "power" Splunk role, should not be able to exploit the vulnerability at will.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17, a low-privileged user who holds the "power" Splunk role could inject arbitrary Search Processing Language (SPL) commands into a Classic Dashboard search. When another user opens the affected dashboard in Splunk Web, those injected commands execute with the viewing user's permissions, potentially allowing the low-privileged user to access stored credentials and write data to indexes.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk Enterprise does not correctly escape user-supplied content when it rewrites a search, which lets the rewritten search include additional SPL commands.
The vulnerability requires another user to open the dashboard in Splunk Web. Consequently, a user who holds the "power" Splunk role should not be able to exploit the vulnerability at will.
For more information see SPL safeguards for risky commands (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.6/best-practices-for-splunk-platform-security/spl-safeguards-for-risky-commands) and Define roles on the Splunk platform with capabilities (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.6/manage-splunk-platform-users-and-roles/define-roles-on-the-splunk-platform-with-capabilities) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.6.1, 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17, a low-privileged user who does not hold the "admin" or "power" Splunk roles could inject a malicious script into the name of a private saved search. If another user subsequently enables, disables, or edits the corresponding platform alert in the Monitoring Console, the injected script executes within that user's browser session, potentially allowing the low-privileged user to view sensitive information or modify data in Splunk Enterprise.
The vulnerability is possible because the Monitoring Console does not safely handle saved-search names in the platform alert workflow.
For more information see Enable and configure platform alerts (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/monitor/10.4/configure-the-monitoring-console/enable-and-configure-platform-alerts) and About configuring role-based user access (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.4/manage-splunk-platform-users-and-roles/about-configuring-role-based-user-access) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17, a user who does not hold the "admin" or "power" Splunk roles could use the apps backup and restore Representational State Transfer (REST) API to prevent subsequent apps backup or restore operations until Splunk Enterprise restarts. This could result in a Denial of Service (DoS).
The vulnerability is possible because the apps backup and restore REST API handlers do not correctly enforce authorization.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17, a user that holds a role with the list_deployment_server capability could access sensitive information from inputs.conf files outside the intended deployment app directory through the Representational State Transfer (REST) API.
The vulnerability is possible because the REST API does not restrict a deployment app name to an existing deployment app before reading input configurations.
For more information see authorize.conf (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/admin-manual/10.4/configuration-file-reference/10.4.4-configuration-file-reference/authorize.conf), Deployment server architecture (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/update-your-deployment/9.0/deployment-server-and-forwarder-management/deployment-server-architecture), and inputs.conf (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/admin-manual/9.4/configuration-file-reference/9.4.16-configuration-file-reference/inputs.conf) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.4, 10.2.8, 10.0.11, and 9.4.16, an unauthenticated user could craft a malicious link that, if opened by an authenticated user, executes arbitrary Search Processing Language (SPL) searches with the victim's permissions. 
Successful exploitation could allow the unauthenticated user to access or modify data, alter Splunk platform configurations, and disrupt operations available to the affected user.
The vulnerability is possible because the Portable Document Format (PDF) generation component processes request data before it rejects deprecated GET requests and does not apply SPL safeguards for risky commands to subsearches.
For more information see Generate PDFs of your reports and dashboards (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/create-dashboards-and-reports/reporting-manual/10.4/report-management/generate-pdfs-of-your-reports-and-dashboards) and SPL safeguards for risky commands (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.4/best-practices-for-splunk-platform-security/spl-safeguards-for-risky-commands) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17, an unauthenticated user could inject arbitrary fields into Splunk Enterprise audit records via the Representational State Transfer (REST) API. 
Successful exploitation could allow the unauthenticated user to forge audit evidence, compromising the integrity of audit reviews and security detections that rely on legacy audit-field parsing.
The vulnerability exists because Splunk Enterprise does not neutralize field delimiters in user-supplied data before writing the data to a legacy audit record. The affected workflow also does not create a corresponding structured audit record.
For more information see Auditing activities in a Splunk platform instance (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.0/audit-activity-in-splunk-enterprise/auditing-activities-in-a-splunk-platform-instance) and About structured audit trail logs (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.2/audit-activity-in-splunk-enterprise/about-structured-audit-trail-logs) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17, an unauthenticated user could access RapidDiag process metadata and log file inventory information through the Representational State Transfer (REST) API.
The vulnerability is possible because certain RapidDiag REST API endpoints accept a factory-default shared key for node authentication, which lets requests bypass Splunk user authentication.
For more information see Using RapidDiag (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/troubleshoot/9.0/contact-splunk-support/using-rapiddiag) and Secure Splunk Enterprise services with pass4SymmKey (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.0/secure-distributed-and-clustered-splunk-environments/secure-splunk-enterprise-services-with-pass4symmkey) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17, a user who does not hold the "admin" or "power" Splunk roles could read private index configuration values for other users through the deployment server Representational State Transfer (REST) API.
The deployment server REST API does not limit a supplied repository location to configured deployment repositories before it reads indexes.conf stanzas.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17, a user holding a role with the edit_token_http capability could create a persistent HTTP Event Collector (HEC) token that cannot be disabled or deleted via the Representational State Transfer (REST) API or Splunk Web. As a result, the token remains active and can continue ingesting events even after administrative attempts to revoke it.
The vulnerability is possible because HTTP Event Collector token creation accepts names that later management operations cannot process.
For more information see authorize.conf (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/admin-manual/10.4/configuration-file-reference/10.4.5-configuration-file-reference/authorize.conf) and Set up and use HTTP Event Collector in Splunk Web (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/get-data-in/get-started-with-getting-data-in/10.6/get-data-with-http-event-collector/set-up-and-use-http-event-collector-in-splunk-web) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.4, 10.2.8, 10.0.11, and 9.4.16, a low-privileged user who holds the "power" Splunk role could inject malicious content into a Splunk Web view. When another authenticated user opens the affected view in Splunk Web, the injected content executes unauthorized JavaScript code within the viewing user's browser session.
The vulnerability is possible because Splunk Web does not properly validate content in a view definition before rendering the view.
For more information see Define roles on the Splunk platform with capabilities (https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/administer/manage-users-and-security/10.2/manage-splunk-platform-users-and-roles/define-roles-on-the-splunk-platform-with-capabilities) in the Splunk documentation.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17, an unauthenticated user could send repeated HTTP PubSub channel subscription requests that cause a Denial of Service (DoS) by permanently increasing memory usage until Splunk Enterprise exhausts available memory. 
The vulnerability affects instances that turn on the [pubsubsvr-http] stanza in server.conf because the HTTP PubSub broker does not release memory associated with a channel after the client disconnects.

In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17, an unauthenticated user who can connect to a Splunk-to-Splunk (S2S) data forwarding receiver could cause the Splunk daemon to terminate unexpectedly. The unexpected termination interrupts data indexing and access to the management API and Splunk Web until the Splunk Enterprise process restarts.
The vulnerability is possible because the S2S data forwarding receiver does not validate an optional field in forwarded event data, which results in a null pointer dereference when the field is missing.
